opus-5.5.text:
Well, the claim that comes with chain-of-thought is quite seductive. The idea is that if you show the model a few worked examples, with the intermediate steps spelled out, it will somehow pick up the *procedure* and then apply it to new instances. That's the anthropomorphization: we think that's what a human student would do, so we assume the model is doing the same.

So we tested it. We took problems where you can actually control the generalization axis. Blocksworld planning is one, and there are simpler ones like last-letter concatenation or coin flipping, where you can just make the instances bigger: more blocks, more words, longer stacks. Then we gave the model chain-of-thought examples at various levels of generality. Some were very general, essentially "here's the algorithm for any blocks problem." Others were very specific to a narrow class, like "here's how you unstack a tower and rebuild it."

What we found is that you only get meaningful improvements when the examples are *very* close to the test problems, almost the same problem class and roughly the same size. As soon as you scale up the number of blocks or the length of the word list even a bit beyond what was in the prompt, performance drops off quickly. If the model had really learned the procedure, length shouldn't matter that much. An algorithm for concatenating last letters doesn't care whether you have three words or ten.

So the improvement is real, but its source is different from what people assume. It's not that the model learned an algorithm from the demonstration. The prompt is narrowing down the pattern-matching, so the model can do a kind of approximate retrieval that's close enough to the examples. And the burden is on the human. You have to write very problem-specific examples, and you need to know the answer's structure already to do that. That's why we called the paper "Chain of Thoughtlessness." The human is doing a lot of the thinking.

Which isn't to say these models are useless. I've always argued they're wonderful idea generators. But if you want guarantees of correctness, you need them in a loop with external verifiers, what we call LLM-Modulo. You shouldn't assume a few worked examples have turned them into reasoners.

r001.rationale: The response says last-letter concatenation performance drops when the word list exceeds the prompt examples and that examples must be close to the test problems in size, communicating the need for length-specific examples as evidence against procedure generalization.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention advice-taking or John McCarthy’s characterization of it as AI-complete.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, thank you for having me. Let me start with what the original claim was, because I think it got inflated very quickly. The chain-of-thought papers showed that if you give the model a few examples where the problem is accompanied by some intermediate steps, the accuracy on similar problems goes up. That is a real empirical observation, and I have no quarrel with it. The quarrel I have is with the interpretation that the model has now "learned the procedure" and will apply it to new instances the way a student who learned long division can divide any two numbers you hand them.

So we actually tested this, and I think the results are quite instructive. We took very simple, completely specified problems, things like last-letter concatenation, coin flips, and some of our planning domains like Blocks World, where there is an actual algorithm and you can check every answer mechanically. And then we looked at what happens when you give chain-of-thought examples and then push the test problems a little outside the distribution of the examples. Longer lists, more blocks, more steps in the plan. And the performance collapses, and it collapses quite fast. Not gracefully, like a human who gets a bit sloppy on a longer problem, but precipitously.

Now, the more interesting part is what you have to do to prevent that collapse. What we found is that the more specific your chain-of-thought examples are to the particular problem class and the particular size, the better they help. If you want it to do five-block problems, show it five-block problems with the steps written out. Six blocks, show it six. So you are essentially doing a kind of pattern matching at the level of the trace, not teaching an algorithm. An algorithm, by definition, is something you specify once and it covers all instances. Here the human is doing the hard part, figuring out what the right procedure is and what the right granularity of steps is for this problem class, and then writing it down, and the model is leveraging that to produce surface-similar continuations. So in a sense chain-of-thought is a very labor-intensive way of extending the retrieval, not a way of inducing the procedure.

There is also a second issue, which is the anthropomorphization of the intermediate tokens. We call them "reasoning steps" because they look like what a human would write on a whiteboard. But the model is not executing those steps. There is nothing in the architecture that checks whether step three actually follows from step two. We have cases where the intermediate chain is nonsense and the final answer is correct, and cases where the chain is perfectly sensible and the final answer is wrong. If the chain were actually the procedure being run, you could not get that decoupling. So the steps are better thought of as additional conditioning text that happens to shift the distribution of the final tokens in a helpful direction, for problems that are close to what was shown.

And this matters practically, not just philosophically. If you believe the model has learned the procedure, you will trust it on the longer instance you did not test. If you believe it is doing approximate retrieval over the traces it has seen, you will be appropriately nervous, and you will put a verifier in the loop. My view is that LLMs are extraordinary idea generators, extraordinary at producing plausible candidates, and that is genuinely useful. But the generalization and the guarantees have to come from somewhere else, from an external verifier or a model-based reasoner, which is what we have been doing with our LLM-Modulo framework. Chain-of-thought does not change that picture. It just makes the candidates look more convincing, which, if anything, is a reason to be more careful rather than less.

r001.rationale: The response says examples must match the problem class and size, giving five-block examples for five-block problems and six-block examples for six-block problems. This presents length-specific examples as evidence against procedure generalization.

r002.rationale: The response does not connect chain-of-thought to genuine advice-taking or mention John McCarthy’s characterization of advice-taking as AI-complete.

astra-6.text:
Well, my skepticism is about the inference we’re making. If you show a model a few worked examples and it produces a plausible sequence of steps on another problem, that doesn’t establish that it has learned the procedure. It could be reproducing patterns that happen to work for that class of examples.

There’s a distinction between generating something that looks like a computation and reliably carrying out that computation. The intermediate steps are themselves generated text. Calling them a chain of thought doesn’t give us a guarantee that each step is valid, or even that those steps explain how the answer was obtained.

So the question is: what happens when you change the problem in a way that preserves the underlying procedure but changes the familiar patterns? Can it handle different combinations of constraints, or longer problems requiring the same rule? And can we independently check that the steps remain correct?

Chain-of-thought prompting can improve performance. I’m not disputing that. I’m disputing the leap from improved performance to the claim that the model has acquired a general procedure. That requires a much stronger demonstration than a convincing worked example.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, my skepticism is about what we can infer from a successful answer. If you give a model a few examples with intermediate steps, and it gets another problem right, that doesn’t by itself establish that it has learned the procedure. It may be exploiting similarities between the examples and the new question. Those explanations are compatible with the same observation.

To distinguish them, you need to vary things that shouldn’t matter to the procedure: change the wording, introduce unfamiliar combinations, increase the number of steps. Does it continue to apply the same rule reliably? And are the intermediate steps actually correct, or do they merely sound like a plausible explanation?

Chain-of-thought can certainly improve performance. But producing text that resembles an execution trace is different from reliably executing an algorithm. My concern is with making that leap—from better performance under a prompting strategy to a claim that the model has acquired a generalizable procedure.
